1231.quote_or_event: “Fareed, those eyes which have enticed the world - I have seen those eyes. Once, they could not endure even a bit of mascara; now, the birds hatch their young in them!”
1231.explanation: Sheikh Farid looks at eyes once so lovely and delicate that they bewitched the world, and sees what has become of them.
1231.tie_back: The Kural's confidante tells the wife that her eyes, which once outshone the flowers, have wept away their beauty; Farid too sets the former loveliness of eyes against their ruin.
1231.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 14) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1231._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable but partial: both mourn eyes whose beauty is gone, but Farid's cause is death and decay, a warning against pride, not weeping for an absent husband.

1232.quote_or_event: “The eyes of the soul-bride are filled with tears; I dwell upon Your Glorious Virtues. How can I meet my Beloved Lord God?”
1232.explanation: In his Barah Maha in Raag Tukhari, Guru Nanak's soul-bride weeps as she remembers her Lord's virtues and asks how she can meet Him.
1232.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her pale, streaming eyes tell everyone that her beloved has stopped being kind to her; Guru Nanak's bride also shows her separation through eyes filled with tears.
1232.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1111, Raag Tukhari, Barah Maha, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1232._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on tearful eyes as the sign of separation, though the Guru's bride does not accuse the Lord of unkindness, and the love is spiritual, not romantic.

1233.quote_or_event: “Fareed, my withered body has become a skeleton; the crows are pecking at my palms. Even now, God has not come to help me; behold, this is the fate of all mortal beings.”
1233.explanation: Sheikh Farid describes a body wasted to bone while the Beloved he longs for has still not come.
1233.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her shoulders, once full on the day of union, have grown thin and loudly announce the separation; Farid's withered body tells the same story of waiting in vain.
1233.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 90) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1233._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable-to-strong fit on a body wasted by unanswered longing, but Farid speaks of old age and longing for God, a spiritual not romantic love, with no image of shoulders.

1234.quote_or_event: “O Lord! Without my Husband, all these adornments are useless.”
1234.explanation: Guru Arjan's bride-soul has put on every ornament, but says none of it means anything while her Husband is away.
1234.tie_back: The Kural's wife, her partner gone, has lost the fullness of her shoulders, and her gold bangles slip from her arms; the Guru's bride likewise finds her ornaments worthless without the Husband.
1234.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1361, Phunhay, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1234._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on adornment losing its point without the beloved, though the Guru speaks of ornaments made useless rather than a body that wastes until bangles slip, and the love is spiritual.

1235.quote_or_event: “If her Husband Lord does not return home, how can the soul-bride find peace? Her body is wasting away with the sorrow of separation.”
1235.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the soul-bride whose Husband has not come home, her body wasting away from the grief of separation.
1235.tie_back: In the Kural the wife's faded shoulders and slipping bangles proclaim to everyone the cruelty of the one who left; Guru Nanak too makes the bride's wasting body the visible sign of the Husband's absence.
1235.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1108, Raag Tukhari, Barah Maha, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1235._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on a body wasted by the husband's absence, but Guru Nanak does not call the Lord cruel, and the love is spiritual, not romantic.

1236.quote_or_event: “Your actions seem so sweet to me.”
1236.explanation: Guru Arjan accepts whatever God does as sweet, the Sikh attitude of living in His will (bhana) without complaint.
1236.tie_back: The Kural's wife is hurt more by hearing others call her husband cruel than by her own wasting; the Sikh devotee likewise refuses to call the Beloved's doings harsh and finds even hardship from Him sweet.
1236.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1236._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable but partial: both refuse to blame the beloved, but the Kural's wife is defending a human husband against gossip, while Guru Arjan is accepting God's will.

1237.quote_or_event: “My mind longs for the Blessed Vision of the Guru's Darshan.”
1237.explanation: These are the opening words of the Shabad Hazare, which Sikh tradition says the young Guru Arjan sent as verse-letters to his father, Guru Ram Das, while he was kept away in Lahore.
1237.tie_back: The Kural's wife urges her heart to go to the hard-hearted one and tell him how her shoulders cry out; Guru Arjan's longing mind likewise speaks across the distance to the one he is parted from.
1237.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1237._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); the letters-from-Lahore story is Sikh tradition, not checked against a source in this session; the fit with a heart sent as messenger is reasonable, and the longing is for the Guru, spiritual rather than romantic.

1238.quote_or_event: “Without water, she cannot live, even for an instant. God knows the suffering of her mind.”
1238.explanation: Guru Nanak compares the soul's love to a fish that cannot live a moment out of water, and says God knows her inner pain.
1238.tie_back: In the Kural the husband remembers that the moment he loosened his embrace, his wife's forehead turned pale; Guru Nanak too speaks of a love that cannot bear a moment's separation, and of a Beloved who knows that pain.
1238.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 60, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1238._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on the beloved who cannot bear even an instant apart and the one who knows her suffering, but it is an analogy for the soul's love of God, with no embrace or pallor.

1239.quote_or_event: “When I could not be with You for just one moment, the Dark Age of Kali Yuga dawned for me.”
1239.explanation: In the Shabad Hazare, Guru Arjan says that even a moment away from the beloved Guru felt like the darkest age of the world.
1239.tie_back: In the Kural even a cool breeze slipping between the embracing couple was enough to make the wife's eyes turn pale; Guru Arjan likewise finds a single moment's separation unbearable.
1239.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1239._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on how even the briefest separation devastates the lover, though the bond is with the Guru, spiritual rather than romantic, and there is no physical image of pallor.

1240.quote_or_event: “I cannot survive without seeing my Beloved. My eyes are welling up with tears.”
1240.explanation: Guru Ram Das says he cannot live without the sight of his Beloved, and his eyes fill with tears.
1240.tie_back: The Kural imagines the wife's eyes falling into distress on seeing what pallor has done to her forehead; in Guru Ram Das too it is the eyes that carry the grief of separation.
1240.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 94, Raag Maajh, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1240._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares sorrowing eyes as the seat of separation's pain, but nothing of the Kural's conceit of one feature grieving at another, and the love is spiritual, not romantic.
